```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)

base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/main/Week7/"
```

# Overview

The task is to record three books on one subject, write the same information by hand in two
formats, load each into R, and decide whether the resulting data frames are identical.

The interesting part is the last step. The two files hold the same facts, but HTML and JSON
represent them differently, so the first comparison fails for reasons that are worth understanding.
This report shows those differences, fixes each one, and ends with the two frames genuinely
identical.

# The Three Books

I chose three books on **data science and statistics**. Two of them have multiple authors, which
satisfies the requirement, and one of those has four. For each book I recorded the title and
authors plus three further attributes: publication year, publisher, and ISBN.

| Title | Authors | Year |
|---|---|---|
| R for Data Science (2nd ed.) | Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, Garrett Grolemund | 2023 |
| An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd ed.) | Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani | 2021 |
| The Art of Statistics | David Spiegelhalter | 2019 |

The ISBNs, publishers and years were checked against the Open Library API, and the author list for
*R for Data Science* against the book's own site, <https://r4ds.hadley.nz>, because Open Library's
record for that edition lists only two of its three authors.

Both files were written by hand and are stored in my GitHub repository, so they are publicly
reachable and this document runs anywhere:
[`books.html`](https://github.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/blob/main/Week7/books.html) and
[`books.json`](https://github.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/blob/main/Week7/books.json).

## The HTML file

```{r}
#| label: show-html
#| class-output: default
read_lines(paste0(base_url, "books.html")) |> cat(sep = "\n")
```

## The JSON file

```{r}
#| label: show-json
#| class-output: default
read_lines(paste0(base_url, "books.json")) |> cat(sep = "\n")
```

The two files are deliberately not written the same way, because the formats do not work the same
way. **HTML has no way to express a list inside a cell**, so the authors are one comma-separated
string. **JSON does**, so the authors are a proper array. That single choice is the main reason the
two data frames will not match at first.

# Loading the HTML

`rvest` reads the page, selects the table element, and converts it to a data frame.

```{r}
#| label: load-html
books_html <- read_html(paste0(base_url, "books.html")) |>
  html_element("table") |>
  html_table()

books_html
```

```{r}
#| label: html-types
tibble(column = names(books_html), type = map_chr(books_html, ~ class(.x)[1])) |> kable()
```

Worth noting: `html_table()` is cleverer than expected. Every value in an HTML file is text, but
the function inspects each column and converts `Year` to an integer on its own. Only the ISBN stays
character, correctly, because the hyphens make it non-numeric.

# Loading the JSON

`jsonlite` reads the file and converts the `books` array directly into a data frame.

```{r}
#| label: load-json
books_json <- fromJSON(paste0(base_url, "books.json"))$books

books_json
```

```{r}
#| label: json-types
tibble(column = names(books_json), type = map_chr(books_json, ~ class(.x)[1])) |> kable()
```

Here the `authors` column is a **list**, not a character vector: each element is a vector of one,
three or four names.

```{r}
#| label: authors-list
books_json$authors
```

# Comparing the Two Data Frames

```{r}
#| label: compare-identical
identical(books_html, books_json)
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-all-equal
all.equal(books_html, books_json)
```

They are **not identical**, and `all.equal()` names exactly why. It returns five messages, but they
come down to **three underlying differences**, and none is a disagreement about the books
themselves:

1. **Column names.** The HTML table uses the header text I wrote, `Title`, `Authors`, `Year`, while
   JSON uses the lowercase keys `title`, `authors`, `year`. Same five columns, different spelling.
2. **The authors column.** Character in one, a list in the other, which is the structural
   difference between the formats.
3. **Object class.** `html_table()` returns a tibble; `fromJSON()` returns a base data frame. This
   accounts for the two `Attributes: Component "class"` messages, since a tibble carries the class
   vector `c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")` against a plain `"data.frame"`. `identical()` compares
   attributes, so this alone would make it `FALSE` even if the contents matched.

```{r}
#| label: show-diffs
tibble(
  difference    = c("Column names", "Authors column type", "Object class"),
  from_html     = c(paste(names(books_html), collapse = ", "),
                    class(books_html$Authors)[1],
                    class(books_html)[1]),
  from_json     = c(paste(names(books_json), collapse = ", "),
                    class(books_json$authors)[1],
                    class(books_json)[1])
) |>
  kable()
```

It is also worth checking what did *not* differ. The values themselves agree, including the
non-ASCII character in "Çetinkaya-Rundel", which survived both the HTML and the JSON round trip:

```{r}
#| label: values-agree
tibble(
  check = c("Rows", "Titles match", "Years match", "ISBNs match", "Non-ASCII name preserved"),
  result = c(
    as.character(nrow(books_html) == nrow(books_json)),
    as.character(identical(books_html$Title, books_json$title)),
    as.character(identical(books_html$Year, books_json$year)),
    as.character(identical(books_html$ISBN, books_json$isbn)),
    as.character(grepl("Çetinkaya-Rundel", books_html$Authors[1]) &
                 any(grepl("Çetinkaya-Rundel", books_json$authors[[1]])))
  )
) |>
  kable()
```

# Reconciling the Differences

Each difference has a decision attached to it.

```{r}
#| label: reconcile
# 1. Column names: lowercase the HTML names to match the JSON keys. JSON keys are
#    the better target because they are already consistent snake_case.
html_tidy <- books_html |>
  rename_with(tolower)

# 2. Authors: collapse the JSON list into one comma-separated string, matching the
#    HTML. I flatten JSON rather than splitting HTML because the goal here is to
#    compare like with like; see the note below on which form is actually better.
json_tidy <- books_json |>
  mutate(authors = map_chr(authors, ~ paste(.x, collapse = ", ")))

# 3. Object class: compare both as plain data frames, so the tibble class does not
#    by itself cause a mismatch.
html_tidy <- as.data.frame(html_tidy)
json_tidy <- as.data.frame(json_tidy)

# Column order is not guaranteed to match either, so align it explicitly.
json_tidy <- json_tidy[, names(html_tidy)]

str(html_tidy)
str(json_tidy)
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-again
all.equal(html_tidy, json_tidy)
```

```{r}
#| label: identical-again
identical(html_tidy, json_tidy)
```

After the three fixes the two data frames are **identical**, which confirms that the files always
held the same information. The disagreement was entirely about representation.

```{r}
#| label: final-frame
html_tidy |> kable()
```

# Conclusions

- **The two files are not identical when first loaded, but the data is the same.** `all.equal()`
  reported three differences: column names, the type of the `authors` column, and the object class.
  After correcting those, both `all.equal()` and `identical()` return `TRUE`.
- **The real difference is structural, and JSON handles it better.** A book can have any number of
  authors. JSON stores that as an array, so *An Introduction to Statistical Learning* keeps four
  distinct author values. HTML has no cell-level list, so the same information becomes the string
  `"Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani"`. The JSON version is closer to
  tidy data, and flattening it to match the HTML actually throws information away.
- **If I needed to analyse these authors**, for example to count books per author, I would go the
  other direction: keep the JSON list and `unnest()` it into one row per book-author pair, rather
  than collapsing it into a string I would then have to split again.
- **Type conversion is not symmetric between the readers.** `html_table()` guessed that `Year` is
  an integer even though HTML stores everything as text, while `fromJSON()` knew it was a number
  because JSON distinguishes numbers from strings. They agreed here, but only by luck of the
  guesser being right. The ISBN is the counter-example worth noticing: both kept it as text, which
  is correct, since `978-1-492-09740-2` would be mangled by any attempt to treat it as a number.
- **The comparison had to be made deliberately.** `identical()` on the two freshly loaded objects
  returns `FALSE` for a reason that has nothing to do with the books: one is a tibble and the other
  is a data frame. A comparison that does not account for class and column order answers a
  different question than the one being asked.
